name.text: Determine sine and cosine from the unit circle

questiontext.text:
Use the unit circle to find the exact values of \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\) for the angle \(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\), measured anticlockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis.

Give your answers in exact form: for example, type sqrt(2) for \(\sqrt{2}\).

(a) \(\cos {@theta@}^\circ = \) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]
(b) \(\sin {@theta@}^\circ = \) [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Worked Solution

On the unit circle (centre \(O\), radius \(1\)), the terminal side of the angle \(\theta\) meets the circle at a point \(P\). The coordinates of \(P\) are \((\cos\theta,\, \sin\theta)\): the \(x\)-coordinate is \(\cos\theta\) and the \(y\)-coordinate is \(\sin\theta\).

[[jsxgraph width="340px" height="340px"]] (function() { var deg = {#theta#}, th = deg*Math.PI/180; var px = Math.cos(th), py = Math.sin(th); var b = JXG.JSXGraph.initBoard(divid, {boundingbox:[-0.35, 1.3, 1.3, -0.35], axis:false, grid:false, keepaspectratio:true, showNavigation:false, showCopyright:false}); b.create('arrow', [[-0.3, 0], [1.25, 0]], {strokeColor:'#444', fixed:true, highlight:false}); b.create('arrow', [[0, -0.3], [0, 1.25]], {strokeColor:'#444', fixed:true, highlight:false}); b.create('text', [1.2, -0.09, 'x'], {fixed:true}); b.create('text', [-0.1, 1.2, 'y'], {fixed:true}); b.create('text', [1.02, -0.09, '1'], {fixed:true}); b.create('text', [-0.09, 1.04, '1'], {fixed:true}); var O = b.create('point', [0, 0], {name:'O', fixed:true, size:2, color:'#222', label:{offset:[-14,-12]}}); b.create('circle', [O, 1], {strokeColor:'#1565c0', strokeWidth:2, fixed:true, highlight:false}); var A = b.create('point', [1, 0], {visible:false, fixed:true}); var P = b.create('point', [px, py], {name:'P', fixed:true, size:4, color:'#c62828', label:{offset:[8,10]}}); b.create('segment', [O, P], {strokeColor:'#c62828', strokeWidth:2, fixed:true}); if (deg > 0) { b.create('angle', [A, O, P], {radius:0.18, name:'θ', fillColor:'#ffb74d', strokeColor:'#ef6c00', fillOpacity:0.35, fixed:true}); } if (deg > 0 && deg < 90) { var Fp = b.create('point', [px, 0], {name:'F', fixed:true, size:2, color:'#444', label:{offset:[4,-12]}}); b.create('segment', [O, Fp], {strokeColor:'#1565c0', strokeWidth:4, fixed:true}); b.create('segment', [Fp, P], {strokeColor:'#2e7d32', strokeWidth:4, fixed:true}); b.create('angle', [P, Fp, O], {type:'square', radius:0.06, name:'', fillOpacity:0, strokeColor:'#444', fixed:true}); b.create('text', [px/2, -0.1, 'cos θ'], {fixed:true, anchorX:'middle', color:'#1565c0'}); b.create('text', [px + 0.04, py/2, 'sin θ'], {fixed:true, anchorX:'left', color:'#2e7d32'}); b.create('text', [px/2 - 0.06, py/2 + 0.07, '1'], {fixed:true, anchorX:'right'}); } })(); [[/jsxgraph]]

Step 1: locate the point \(P\) for \(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\). [[if test="is(theta=0)"]]An angle of \(0^\circ\) does not turn at all, so the terminal side lies along the positive \(x\)-axis and meets the circle at \(P = (1,\, 0)\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(theta=90)"]]An angle of \(90^\circ\) is a quarter turn, so the terminal side lies along the positive \(y\)-axis and meets the circle at \(P = (0,\, 1)\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(theta>0 and theta<90)"]]\(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\) is between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\), so \(P\) is in Quadrant I, where both coordinates are positive.[[/if]]

[[if test="is(theta>0 and theta<90)"]]

Step 2: draw the right-angled triangle. Drop a perpendicular from \(P\) to the \(x\)-axis at \(F\). In the right-angled triangle \(OFP\), the hypotenuse is the radius, \(OP = 1\), and the angle at \(O\) is \(\theta\). So

\[ \cos\theta = \frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{OF}{1} = OF, \qquad \sin\theta = \frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{FP}{1} = FP. \]

The horizontal side \(OF\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\), and the vertical side \(FP\) is its \(y\)-coordinate.

Step 3: use the special triangle for \({@theta@}^\circ\). [[if test="is(theta=45)"]]A \(45^\circ\) right-angled triangle is isosceles, so \(OF = FP\). With legs of \(1\), the hypotenuse is \(\sqrt{2}\). Dividing every side by \(\sqrt{2}\) makes the hypotenuse \(1\), so each leg is \(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(theta=30 or theta=60)"]]Half of an equilateral triangle with sides \(2\) has sides \(1\), \(\sqrt{3}\) and \(2\), with angles \(30^\circ\), \(60^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\). Halving every side makes the hypotenuse \(1\), so the sides become \(\dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(1\). The shorter side \(\dfrac{1}{2}\) is opposite the \(30^\circ\) angle, and the longer side \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) is opposite the \(60^\circ\) angle.[[/if]] [[if test="is(theta=30)"]]Here \(\theta = 30^\circ\), so the side opposite \(\theta\) is \(FP = \dfrac{1}{2}\), and the side next to it is \(OF = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).[[/if]] [[if test="is(theta=60)"]]Here \(\theta = 60^\circ\), so the side opposite \(\theta\) is \(FP = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\), and the side next to it is \(OF = \dfrac{1}{2}\).[[/if]]

Step 4: read off the ratios.

[[else]]

Step 2: read off the ratios from the coordinates of \(P\).

[[/if]] \[ \cos {@theta@}^\circ = x = {@cos_theta@}, \qquad \sin {@theta@}^\circ = y = {@sin_theta@}. \]

[[if test="is(theta=90)"]]Since \(\tan\theta = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\) and \(\cos 90^\circ = 0\), \(\tan 90^\circ\) is undefined.[[else]]It follows that \(\tan {@theta@}^\circ = \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = {@tan_theta@}\).[[/if]]

[[if test="is(theta>0 and theta<90)"]]In the diagram, the blue side \(OF\) is \(\cos\theta\) and the green side \(FP\) is \(\sin\theta\).[[else]]In the diagram, \(P\) lies on an axis, so one of its coordinates is \(0\) and the other is \(1\).[[/if]]

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text: That is the value of \(\sin\theta\), not \(\cos\theta\). On the unit circle, \(\cos\theta\) is the \(x\)-coordinate of \(P\): the horizontal distance from \(O\).

truefeedback.text: Your value is twice too big. On the unit circle the hypotenuse is the radius, which is \(1\), so scale the special triangle down until its hypotenuse is \(1\).

falsefeedback.text: Find the point \(P\) for \(\theta = {@theta@}^\circ\) on the unit circle. \(\cos\theta\) is its \(x\)-coordinate: use the special triangle with hypotenuse \(1\), or the point where the circle meets an axis.

truefeedback.text: That is the value of \(\cos\theta\), not \(\sin\theta\). On the unit circle, \(\sin\theta\) is the \(y\)-coordinate of \(P\): the height of \(P\) above the \(x\)-axis.
